issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Arjun, a 53‑year‑old South‑Asian painter, had spent the last two decades coaxing pigment onto canvas in the cramped loft above his parents’ apartment. His hands, once steady as a sculptor’s, now trembled when a sudden thud rattled the floor, and he would pause mid‑stroke to scan the shadows for a hidden danger. The day he was 35, he was a civilian in a war zone that had been turned into a battlefield of artillery and bombs. He recalls the heat of the blast, the acrid scent of burning plastic that filled the air, and the terrifying feeling of losing control as the ground beneath him shattered. That single incident planted the seeds of the three triggers that would haunt him: the smell of smoke, the sharp sound of an explosion, and the crushing loss of control. The next morning, as he opened his kitchen window, a faint, familiar odor of charred metal drifted in from the street, and his heart leapt. The smell, a direct reminder of that night, sent his brain into a state of hypervigilance, his ears prickling at every distant rumble. He found himself tightening his shoulders, his pulse racing, as if the world were still a battlefield. In the same instant, the memory of the explosion flooded him, his body automatically adopting the tense posture he had assumed during the attack. He felt a cold grief wash over him, a sense that the story was so unreal it seemed impossible that it had ever occurred to him. The mere scent made him re‑experience the loss of control he had endured, reinforcing his belief that the world was an ever‑dangerous place and that nothing in his life held meaning beyond that night. Arjun had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the work that defined him; each brushstroke felt like a task in a war zone. This negative appraisal pushed him into a web of maladaptive strategies. He began to ruminate endlessly, revisiting the war as if it were a puzzle he needed to solve, and he kept himself perpetually busy, chasing deadlines for commissions that could no longer satisfy the emptiness inside. He avoided news reports about similar events, fearing that hearing about other bombings would trigger his hypervigilance and plunge him back into that night. Every time he avoided a news segment, his mind returned to the memory, amplifying the grief and reinforcing the sense that the world was unsafe. The negative appraisal also heightened his awareness of the triggers; he became more alert to any scent or sound that might echo the war’s chaos. The vivid memories of that night did more than just fill his thoughts; they intensified his threat appraisal. Whenever a memory surfaced, he felt his body tense, his eyes darting, and his hands shaking—a bodily reenactment that made the threat feel imminent. The startle response to ordinary sounds, once a minor annoyance, grew into a frantic reaction that left him exhausted. Grief over the memory reinforced his belief that life had lost meaning, making the memory itself more potent. In turn, the constant threat appraisal drove him to further maladaptive behaviors: the more he tried to stay alert, the more he worked himself to exhaustion, and the more he ruminated, the more the memory surfaced, completing a vicious cycle. The avoidance strategies he adopted also fed back into the loop. By staying busy, he forced himself to suppress the memory, but the suppression manifested as a sharper focus on sensory details—any odd sound or scent would immediately shatter his concentration, pulling him back into the moment of war. Avoiding the news kept his mind in a state of alertness, because he felt the world was more dangerous the longer he stayed uninformed. These behaviors kept his threat appraisal high, and each time a memory came to him, the sense of threat intensified, re‑igniting his avoidance and rumination. Thus, the triggers, memory, threat, negative appraisal, and maladaptive strategies were all locked in a self‑reinforcing spiral that had gradually eroded his ability to work and to enjoy his family life. Now, Arjun sits in the studio, the canvas before him blank, the smell of fresh oil paint in the air. He feels a knot tighten in his chest as he hears the distant sound of traffic, and he wonders whether he will be able to finish the portrait he began last month. The relentless loop has taken a toll on his marriage; his wife notices his growing irritability and his increasing reluctance to leave the house. He has finally decided to seek help because each day he feels the world slipping farther away, and he fears that if he does nothing, he will be forced to abandon his art entirely. In the quiet of the studio, he clutches his brush, hoping that therapy might break the chain and restore a sense of meaning and safety to his life.
